lesson_title: Locked Up by Their Own Country
hook_text: They were American citizens. They had done nothing wrong. They were given a week to pack.
clip_script: California, 1942. A notice is nailed to a telephone pole. All persons of Japanese ancestry must leave. Two months earlier, Japan bombed Pearl Harbour, and fear swept the country. Rumours said Japanese Americans were spies. The government's own reports said they were loyal. It made no difference. About 120 000 people, two thirds of them American citizens, were forced from their homes. They could take only what they could carry. Some slept in horse stables at a racetrack. Then trains took them to ten camps behind barbed wire. Meanwhile, their sons joined the army and became one of the most decorated units in American history. Not one Japanese American was convicted of spying. It took until 1988 for the government to say sorry. What caused it? An official inquiry gave three answers: race prejudice, war hysteria and a failure of leadership.
visual_style: A paper notice flutters on a pole; suitcases with numbered tags; rows of barracks under watchtowers in a dusty desert; a soldier's medal; a signed letter with the date 1988.
pacing: Measured throughout, slowing for the final three causes.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to see how this happened and how it was challenged.
